"Look, Harsha," said Gargi didi, holding up one coconut laddoo. "Eat this one now, or wait till I finish folding the clothes and get two."
"Two!" said Harsha. He sat on the sofa and stared at the laddoo on the plate.
"Count the socks with me?" Gargi asked.
Harsha counted one sock. Then he looked at the plate again. His fingers crept closer.
"Harsha, two is more," she said.
"This one," he said, and pushed the whole laddoo into his mouth.
Gargi laughed. "Okay. Just one, then."
Harsha chewed, looked at the empty plate and frowned. "Where's my other one?"

qa.q: What did Gargi offer Harsha?
qa.a: Gargi offered one coconut laddoo now, or two if Harsha would wait till she finished folding the clothes.

qa.q: Why did eating the laddoo at once feel right to Harsha?
qa.a: Harsha felt impatient and eager, because the laddoo sat right there on the plate while the second one was only a promise after a pile of clothes.

qa.q: At which moment could Gargi have helped Harsha hold on, and how?
qa.a: When his fingers crept towards the plate, she could have moved it out of sight and made the sock counting a real game, so he was not staring at the laddoo.

qa.q: How does Gargi seem to take Harsha's choice?
qa.a: Gargi laughs and lets him have his one without scolding, as if she knows waiting is very hard for a child as small as Harsha.

grounding: Illustrates a young child who cannot hold out for two sweets and eats the single one in front of him right away.

Note for Nitin's parents, Tuesday
At snack time we played a waiting game. Each child got a star sticker on a card: leave it there until the bell and get a second star, or peel it off now.
Nitin touched the shiny star and peeled it off within a minute. He pressed it on his shirt. When the bell rang and the others got two, his face fell and he asked for another.
Waiting is hard for everyone at four. Tomorrow we will try again with the card face-down and a song to sing.
Hafsa, KG teacher

qa.q: What did Nitin do with the star sticker?
qa.a: Nitin peeled it off within a minute and pressed it on his shirt.

qa.q: Why did peeling the star straight away make sense to Nitin?
qa.a: Nitin felt eager for the shiny star right under his fingers, and the bell felt far away; when the others got two, his face fell because he was disappointed.

qa.q: Which change does Hafsa plan, and why might it work?
qa.a: Putting the card face-down and adding a song takes the star out of view and fills the wait, so Nitin is not stuck staring at the prize.

qa.q: How does Hafsa see Nitin's quick choice?
qa.a: Hafsa does not treat it as naughtiness; the note says waiting is hard for everyone at four and plans another try.

grounding: Shows a four-year-old at school taking the small reward at once instead of waiting for the bigger one.

The village fair was loud with drums. Shankar kaka held Madhav's hand near the sweet stall.
"A small peppermint now," kaka said, "or the big jalebi after the bullock race. Your choice."
Madhav looked at the peppermint jar. The race had not even started. The jalebi pan was far away, behind a crowd of people.
"Peppermint!" he said, and held out his hand.
He sucked it hard while the carts thundered past. Walking home, he saw another boy with a huge orange jalebi and tugged kaka's sleeve, his lip wobbling.

qa.q: Which two treats did Shankar kaka offer Madhav?
qa.a: A small peppermint now, or the big jalebi after the bullock race.

qa.q: What made the peppermint feel like the better deal to Madhav in that moment?
qa.a: The jar was right in front of him, while the race had not started and the jalebi pan was hidden behind a crowd, so later felt too far away to matter.

qa.q: What could Shankar kaka try at the next fair so Madhav can wait?
qa.a: Kaka could walk him to watch the jalebis frying and make cheering for the race the waiting game, so the big treat feels close and the time passes.

qa.q: What might Shankar kaka feel when Madhav tugs his sleeve on the way home?
qa.a: Kaka may feel tender and a little sorry, seeing Madhav wish for the jalebi he gave up, and may not want to scold a small child for it.

grounding: Depicts a small child at a village fair choosing a small sweet at once over a bigger one after the race.

At the bakery near the bus stop in Seville, Diego held up the paper bag. "Layla, one churro now, or two when we get home after the bus."
Layla, five, looked at the bag. The sugar smell was everywhere. "Home is far," she said.
"Only four stops."
"Now!" She grabbed one and ate it before the bus came.
At home, Diego put two churros on his own plate. Layla stared at them, then at her sticky fingers. "That's not fair. You got more."
"You chose, Layla."

qa.a: Layla felt impatient for a churro with the sugar smell everywhere and home far away, then upset when she saw two churros on Diego's plate and said it wasn't fair.

qa.q: What could Diego try next time to help Layla wait?
qa.a: He could keep the bag out of sight and play a counting game for the four stops, so the wait feels short and home feels close.

qa.q: How might Diego feel when Layla says it's not fair?
qa.a: Diego may feel a bit annoyed, since Layla made the choice, but also sorry to see her upset over the two churros on his plate.

grounding: It shows a young child who cannot wait for a bigger treat and grabs the smaller one at once, then feels resentful later.

In the children's dental clinic in Pune, the receptionist, Swati, held out a sheet of dinosaur stickers. "Yogesh, you can have one sticker now, or two after the doctor checks your teeth."
Yogesh, five, didn't even look at the doctor's door. "Now!" He peeled one and stuck it on his shirt.
After the check-up, the girl before him came out with two stickers on her hand.
Yogesh's face went red. "I want two also!"
"You took yours already," Swati said gently.
He folded his arms and wouldn't look at anyone all the way to the car.

qa.a: Swati could show the two stickers on a card beside the doctor's door, so the later reward feels real and close, not far away.

qa.a: It feels unfair and upsetting to him, and the folded arms show his resentment, even though he chose one earlier.
